title: Civil and structural engineering
note: Structures carry loads safely to the ground. Dead loads are permanent, live loads change, and environmental loads include wind, snow, and earthquakes. Beams resist by bending, arches mainly by compression, and cables by tension; foundations spread the final load into soil or rock.

read.title: How structures carry loads
text: Every structure has one job: carry its loads safely to the ground. Engineers sort those loads into dead loads, such as the weight of beams and slabs, live loads, such as people and traffic, and environmental loads from wind, snow, and earthquakes. They then trace a load path from roof to foundation and make sure every link can carry its share.

A beam carries load by bending. Under a downward load the top of a simply supported beam is squeezed and the bottom is stretched, with zero stress at the neutral axis between them. Material far from that axis works hardest, which is why I-beams put most of their steel in the flanges. Stiffness grows with the cube of depth, so a beam twice as deep is eight times as stiff.

Other forms avoid bending. An arch turns load into compression and pushes outward at its supports. A suspension bridge hangs its deck from cables in pure tension, draped over towers in compression, which is why it can span the farthest.
At the bottom, foundations spread the load. Strong soil allows shallow spread footings; weak soil calls for deep piles.
